sections.h2: Which Oregon law governs landlords and tenants?
sections.html:
Chapter 90 of the Oregon Revised Statutes, the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, covers most residential rentals. Mobile home and floating home parks have their own section, and some rules, such as the rent cap, say outright that they do not apply there.

Cities can add to the state rules. Portland, for example, requires landlords to pay relocation assistance in several situations, and an annotation to ORS 90.427 notes that the state section does not preempt local relocation ordinances (Owen v. City of Portland, 2020). A landlord selling a rental should check both layers before giving any notice.

Oregon caps yearly rent increases for most tenancies, and the state publishes the percentage each year. For tenancies covered by ORS 90.323, the cap is the lesser of 10 percent or 7 percent plus the consumer price index. The Department of Administrative Services set it at 9.5 percent for 2026 and 10 percent for 2027.

The same statute sets process rules:

  • Written notice at least 90 days before the increase takes effect, or 7 days for a week-to-week tenancy.
  • No increase during the first year of a tenancy that is not week-to-week.
  • No more than one increase in any 12-month period.
  • The notice must state the amount, the new rent and the effective date.

A building is exempt from the cap if its first certificate of occupancy was issued less than 15 years before the notice. Regulated affordable housing has its own exemption. A landlord who breaks the cap owes the tenant three months of rent plus actual damages. The state rent stabilization page carries the current figure.

Oregon allows only the fees that ORS 90.302 and ORS 90.260 list, and each one has to appear in the written rental agreement. A landlord who charges a prohibited fee owes the tenant twice the actual damages or $300, whichever is greater.

ChargeLimit in the statute
Late rent, flat feeOne reasonable flat amount per rental period, once rent is not received by the fourth day
Late rent, daily feeStarts on day 5, no more than 6 percent of the flat fee per day
Late rent, percentage fee5 percent of periodic rent for each five-day period or part of one
Tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarmUp to $250
Abandoning a fixed-term tenancyUp to 1.5 times monthly rent
Repeated rule violationsMostly capped at $50, with prior written warnings; smoking and unauthorized dangerous pets capped at $250

Unpaid late fees cannot be the basis for a nonpayment termination, though they can support a for-cause termination. A landlord who changes the late fee structure in a periodic tenancy must give 30 days of written notice. The rules are in ORS 90.260 and ORS 90.302.

ORS 90.300 gives the landlord 31 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant hands over possession to return the deposit or send an itemized written accounting for what was kept. The rule also covers last month's rent deposits.

  • A landlord may keep only what is reasonably necessary for unpaid rent, other defaults, and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear.
  • After the first year of tenancy, a landlord generally cannot require a new or increased deposit, apart from specific cases such as agreeing to allow a pet.
  • No pet deposit may be charged for a service animal or companion animal that a tenant with a disability needs as a reasonable accommodation.
  • A landlord who misses the deadline or withholds in bad faith owes the tenant twice the amount withheld.

For a seller, the statute also makes whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends answerable to the tenant for the deposit. Track deposits and prepaid rent and credit them in the closing paperwork so the new owner is not surprised.

sections.h2: What counts as retaliation by a landlord?
sections.html:
Once a tenant takes a protected action, an Oregon landlord cannot raise rent, cut services, serve a termination notice or file or threaten a possession case in response. ORS 90.385 lists the protected actions.

  • Complaining to a government agency about a code violation that affects health or safety.
  • Making a good-faith complaint to the landlord about the tenancy.
  • Joining or organizing a tenants' union.
  • Testifying against the landlord in a court, agency or legislative proceeding.
  • Winning a possession case within the previous six months, unless the win came only from improper service or too little notice.

The statute gives the landlord some exceptions, such as a complaint made in an unreasonable manner or a tenant who was behind on rent when the notice was served. Retaliation is also a defense in a possession case, so a notice served soon after a complaint deserves a second look before a sale is planned around it.

A landlord must keep the unit habitable under ORS 90.320, and may enter to inspect, repair, supply services or show the unit to prospective buyers under ORS 90.322. Both duties run together once a rental is on the market.

Habitability includes weather protection, plumbing, hot and cold running water, adequate heat, electrical lighting, safe grounds, garbage receptacles, floors, walls and stairs in good repair, and a working smoke alarm at the start of the tenancy.

Insurance rules are in ORS 90.222. A landlord who requires renter's liability insurance must put that in the written agreement, carry comparable coverage and show proof on request. A month-to-month tenant gets at least 30 days of written notice before the requirement is added.

Portland requires a landlord to pay mandatory relocation assistance in several situations: a no-cause termination, a qualifying landlord reason for ending a tenancy, a rent increase of 10 percent or more in 12 months, and a substantial change in lease terms.

  • Studio or single room occupancy: $2,900.
  • One bedroom: $3,300.
  • Two bedrooms: $4,200.
  • Three bedrooms or larger: $4,500.

The landlord pays, the tenant must get at least 90 days of written notice that describes the right, and the landlord has 30 days to report each payment to the Portland Housing Bureau. A landlord who does not comply can owe up to three times the monthly rent plus actual damages, the relocation amount and attorney fees. Exemptions exist and most require a filing, so read the city's relocation page before relying on one.

sections.h2: Handling tenants when you sell the rental
sections.html:
Under ORS 90.427, a sale counts as a qualifying landlord reason only when the buyer intends in good faith to live in the home. ORS 90.300 makes whoever holds the landlord's interest answerable for the deposit, and ORS 90.427 limits when a month-to-month tenancy can be ended after the first year.

  • Settle the deposit and prepaid rent in writing.
  • Give showing notice that follows ORS 90.322.
  • Check any rent increase notice against the 90-day and once-a-year limits.
  • If a qualifying reason applies, such as a buyer who will live in the home, follow the notice and payment steps in our eviction guide and watch the three-month penalty for a wrongful termination.

Some owners prefer to skip those steps and sell to a buyer who will keep the tenant in place. We buy houses with tenants in Oregon, and you can ask us what that looks like for your lease.

faqs.q: How much can my landlord raise my rent in Oregon?
faqs.a: The cap for 2026 is 9.5 percent and for 2027 it is 10 percent, for tenancies covered by ORS 90.323. The landlord must give 90 days of written notice, cannot raise rent in the first year, and can raise it only once in 12 months. Buildings under 15 years old are exempt.

faqs.q: How soon must a landlord return a security deposit in Oregon?
faqs.a: Within 31 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant gives up possession. The landlord must return the deposit or send an itemized written accounting. A landlord who withholds in bad faith can owe twice the amount withheld.

faqs.q: Can a landlord charge a late fee in Oregon?
faqs.a: Yes, but only if the written rental agreement provides for it and rent is not received by the fourth day of the rental period. The fee must be one of the three structures in ORS 90.260: a flat fee, a daily fee starting on day 5, or 5 percent of rent per five-day period.

faqs.q: Does a new owner have to honor an existing lease in Oregon?
faqs.a: ORS 90.300 makes the holder of the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends answerable to the tenant for the deposit, and ORS 90.427 limits ending a tenancy early to listed reasons with set notice. Ask an attorney how those rules apply to your lease.

faqs.q: Is Portland relocation assistance required when I sell?
faqs.a: Only if a triggering event applies, such as a qualifying landlord reason for ending the tenancy, and no exemption covers you. The amounts run from $2,900 for a studio to $4,500 for three bedrooms or larger, and the tenant needs at least 90 days of notice.
